title: DynFO maintenance of red-predecessor parity
formal: Does there exist a DynFO program that maintains the Boolean query |\(\{y\in D:\exists x\in D (R(x)\land E(x,y))\}|\equiv 1\) mod 2 under arbitrary single-tuple insertions and deletions in a directed edge relation \(E\subseteq D^{2}\) and a red-vertex relation \(R\subseteq D\)? Use one fixed finite auxiliary relational vocabulary and fixed first-order update formulas for every finite domain D. All input and auxiliary relations are empty initially, and there are no built-in order or arithmetic relations. The program must be correct after every finite sequence of updates, with no bound on the length of that sequence.
context:
Parity of a directly stored unary set can be maintained by tracking individual membership changes. Here a red-vertex update can change the coverage of many successors, while overlapping red neighborhoods mean that not every incident successor actually changes status. The queried parity concerns covered vertices, not the number of red vertices or red incident edges.

The paper proves that ParityExists cannot be maintained with quantifier-free first-order update rules, even with stronger initialization allowances. Its open question permits full first-order quantification and auxiliary relations of any fixed finite arity, so that lower bound is insufficient.

The source studies the variant counting only covered vertices whose indegree is at most a threshold. It proves DynFO results when the threshold grows logarithmically, with the stated built-in order/BIT conventions and an active-domain version without them. This is a filtered counting query, not a solution of unrestricted ParityExists.

The query has the form of a parity quantifier outside an existential quantifier. Understanding it is a basic obstacle to classifying which queries from first-order logic with parity can be maintained by ordinary first-order updates. Solving this one query alone is not asserted to settle that broader inclusion.
why: Would clarify whether first-order dynamic maintenance can express a basic combination of existential coverage and parity counting, beyond the already understood parity of a directly stored set.

references.title: Dynamic Complexity of Parity Exists Queries
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 15; PDF page 15

definitions: The domain D is a fixed finite set throughout a run; updates do not create or delete vertices. An element y is covered when at least one red predecessor x has an arc \(x\to y\). A covered vertex is counted once, regardless of how many red predecessors it has, and it need not itself be red. E is a binary relation, so loops are allowed; R is unary. The four update types are \(ins_{E}(u,v), del_{E}(u,v), ins_{R}(u)\), and \(del_{R}(u)\). Insertions of present tuples and deletions of absent tuples leave the input relation unchanged and are also allowed. A program chooses finitely many auxiliary relation symbols S, each of a fixed finite arity, including a distinguished zero-ary answer bit Ans. For each S and update type \(\delta\) it supplies a first-order formula \(\varphi _{S,\delta}(\bar\{p\};\bar\{z\})\), where p̄ are the changed tuple’s parameters and z̄ has the arity of S. The formula may use equality, the current input and auxiliary relations, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual domain elements. It has no parity/counting quantifier, quantification over sets, function symbol or built-in numeric relation. After update \(\delta (\bar\{a\})\), each auxiliary relation becomes \(\{\bar\{b\}:(I,A)\models \varphi _{S,\delta}(\bar\{a\};\bar\{b\})\}\), evaluated on the old input I and old auxiliary state A. All auxiliary updates occur simultaneously, alongside the specified input change. Empty initialization makes Ans false, correctly answering the empty covered set. The program’s formulas and arities are independent of |D| and of the update history. The number and arities of auxiliary relations are unrestricted finite constants chosen by the program; thus it may use polynomially many auxiliary bits, with its own fixed polynomial exponent. DynFO measures expressibility of these updates, rather than sequential constant-time execution of a formula on a Turing machine.
answer_criterion: A positive answer is a finite collection of first-order update formulas and a proof of correctness from empty initialization for every finite domain and every finite update sequence. A negative answer must show that every such program, allowing arbitrary fixed auxiliary arities, fails on some domain and sequence. A lower bound only for quantifier-free formulas or a fixed arity, a program requiring unrestricted initial advice, or an algorithm for a bounded-degree variant does not settle the stated DynFO question.
